findings.affected_section: Sections 6, D4, D7, 13 and 14 — Compose modes, profiles and CLI
findings.claim: The plan does not define deterministic Compose merge/profile semantics or an exclusive mode-convergence algorithm.
findings.evidence: 07_FULL_PLAN.md:175-200 defines mock, real-dev and gate conceptually; 433 names local Compose overrides/profiles; 531-533 exposes start/stop commands; 560-562 proposes three Compose files. It never fixes the -f ordering, profile membership of every service, project-name source, environment-file precedence, rendered service matrix, or mock-to-real and real-to-mock transition behavior. Line 487 requires polling to stop but does not specify how services hidden by a different profile are found and stopped.
findings.impact: A mode switch can leave the bridge polling while mock mode appears active, run mocks and real adapters together, retain stale containers, or inherit an unintended port, network, volume or environment value through Compose merging. This defeats the manual real-traffic gate and makes start/stop non-idempotent.
findings.required_resolution: Define one canonical Compose invocation per command with fixed project name, ordered files, profiles and env sources. Publish the exact expected service/network/volume set for each mode. Make the wrapper converge from any prior mode by explicitly detecting and stopping incompatible services, reject simultaneous modes, and verify the rendered configuration before mutation. The supported interface must not start a profiled real service by directly targeting its service name without the real-dev gate.
findings.acceptance_test: Test fresh mock, repeated mock, fresh real-dev, repeated real-dev, mock-to-real, real-to-mock, Docker Desktop restart, and stop from both modes. For every case assert the exact running service set, absence of incompatible services, fixed project labels, expected networks and bindings, and zero bridge polling after stop or mock convergence. Negative tests must reject mixed mode flags and any rendered configuration outside the approved matrix.

findings.affected_section: D6 and section 17 — startup, health and migrations
findings.claim: Startup is expressed as prose ordering rather than an enforceable health and migration dependency graph.
findings.evidence: 07_FULL_PLAN.md:455-465 says to start PostgreSQL and migrations, then n8n, then mocks, but specifies no healthchecks, migration one-shot service contract, depends_on conditions, readiness timeout or restart policy. Line 649 asks for migrations, fault atomicity and persistence only at the verification-matrix level.
findings.impact: Cold starts and restarts can race PostgreSQL initialization, migrations or n8n readiness. A failed migration may still allow n8n or the bridge to start, and an automatically restarted bridge may deliver traffic to a partially initialized application.
findings.required_resolution: Specify PostgreSQL health, a versioned one-shot migration service that must exit successfully, n8n application readiness, and bridge/mock dependencies. Define restart policies, stop grace periods, bounded readiness timeouts and wrapper exit behavior. One-shot migration and backup jobs must not restart indefinitely. Application components must tolerate or fail closed on dependency restart.
findings.acceptance_test: Inject slow PostgreSQL startup, failed and partially applied migrations, delayed n8n readiness, and forced PostgreSQL/n8n restarts. start must remain bounded, return nonzero on failure, never start the bridge before schema and n8n readiness, and become healthy without manual container-order commands after recoverable dependency restarts.

findings.affected_section: Sections 5, 6, D6 and 17 — PostgreSQL boundaries and migrations
findings.claim: The plan does not define the required PostgreSQL database, role, schema, ownership and migration-authority model.
findings.evidence: 07_FULL_PLAN.md:146 depicts one PostgreSQL service; 182 mentions schema and migrations; 458 only says to start PostgreSQL and migrations; 649 requires roles/grants and fault atomicity. No role matrix, database/schema ownership, search_path, default privileges, bootstrap credential, runtime credential, migration credential, or existing-volume migration behavior is specified. 06_ARCHITECTURE_BASELINE.md requires separate metadata/app/memory database boundaries.
findings.impact: Implementation can collapse n8n metadata, application data and memory into an overprivileged role or schema. Runtime compromise could modify metadata or cross isolation boundaries. Init scripts that work only on an empty volume can also create a false green result while upgrades of persistent volumes remain broken.
findings.required_resolution: Define a least-privilege matrix for n8n metadata, application state, memory/dedup state, bootstrap and migrations. Specify database/schema owners, CONNECT/USAGE/DML/DDL grants, default privileges, search_path, credential separation and prohibited attributes such as SUPERUSER, CREATEDB and CREATEROLE. Separate first-volume bootstrap from checksummed, ordered, transactional migrations that run on existing volumes.
findings.acceptance_test: On both empty and previously populated volumes, assert role attributes and effective grants from every runtime identity; cross-boundary reads/writes and DDL must fail. Re-running migrations must be idempotent, a fault-injected migration must roll back atomically, migration-history checksums must match, and n8n/app workflows must still operate with only their documented privileges.

findings.affected_section: Sections 8, D4, D6 and 17 — n8n runtime contract
findings.claim: The n8n contract omits exact database configuration, execution mode, process topology, encryption-key initialization and persistent-directory ownership.
findings.evidence: 07_FULL_PLAN.md:246 lists N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY; 457 creates DB/encryption secrets; 459 starts n8n; 460 creates the owner; 650 asks for owner/2FA and import/export. No exact-version-supported n8n configuration variables, explicit regular versus queue execution decision, Redis/worker topology, fail-closed key check, key-before-first-boot rule, container UID/GID, persistent path ownership, or proof that SQLite fallback is impossible appears in the plan.
findings.impact: An inherited or mistaken queue configuration can leave executions unprocessed without Redis/workers. Missing PostgreSQL configuration can silently select unintended storage. A regenerated or mismatched encryption key makes credentials unreadable, while root-owned restored files can make the container fail only after restart.
findings.required_resolution: Define an allowlisted n8n configuration for the pinned version. Explicitly select single-process regular execution for this lab, or fully specify pinned Redis and worker services if queue mode is required. Require PostgreSQL explicitly and reject SQLite artifacts. Generate and bind one persistent encryption key before first boot, fail closed when it is absent or changed, and define supported secret injection, container identity, writable paths and ownership. Verify all variable names and defaults against the exact pinned n8n release before image acceptance.
findings.acceptance_test: A redacted rendered configuration and runtime assertions must prove the selected execution mode, PostgreSQL backend and absence of unintended queue/SQLite state. Create a credential and workflow, restart n8n and Docker Desktop, and prove execution plus credential decryptability. Missing or substituted encryption key must stop the stack with a diagnostic rather than create a new instance. Restored volumes must be writable by the documented non-root identity.

findings.affected_section: Sections 10, D5, D10, 13 and 15 — upgrades and rollback
findings.claim: The promised update operation has no migration-safe upgrade or rollback procedure.
findings.evidence: 07_FULL_PLAN.md:449 proposes versions; 516 requires an update runbook; 325 says to return to the last pinned Compose/image inventory on an unhealthy container. The plan never distinguishes an image restart from an n8n schema migration or PostgreSQL major-version upgrade, and never forbids launching an older application against a database already migrated by a newer one.
findings.impact: Rolling an image digest backward may not roll the database schema backward. A PostgreSQL major image may reject the existing data directory. The documented recovery can therefore fail precisely when needed or expose persistent data to an unsupported downgrade.
findings.required_resolution: Define separate n8n patch/minor and PostgreSQL major upgrade state machines with from/to digest compatibility evidence. Before mutation, produce and restore-test the DB, n8n data and encryption-key pair. Stage upgrades against cloned/restored volumes, record migrations, and promote only after acceptance. Rollback must restore the pre-upgrade database/volumes and matching key; never run an older n8n against migrated state. PostgreSQL major upgrades must use an explicitly supported logical restore or pg_upgrade procedure rather than reusing the data directory blindly.
findings.acceptance_test: Run a supported n8n upgrade on an isolated clone, inject failure after migration begins, and demonstrate restoration of the old digest with pre-upgrade schema and decryptable credentials. Separately test the documented PostgreSQL major-upgrade path and prove that direct reuse of an incompatible data directory is rejected before startup.

findings.affected_section: Sections 7, 10 and D7 — bridge offset persistence and backup consistency
findings.claim: Bridge offset persistence is required but has no defined durable store or consistent backup boundary.
findings.evidence: 07_FULL_PLAN.md:218 and 224 require a saved, atomically updated offset; 153-157 lists persistent volumes but none for bridge state; 483 requires offset persistence. Backup steps 312-319 may stop only n8n and do not explicitly stop the bridge or bind its offset state to the PostgreSQL/dedup snapshot.
findings.impact: Restart or restore can lose the accepted offset, replay a large update range, or restore offsets and dedup state from different moments. Deduplication may limit side effects but does not make the lifecycle reproducible and can generate confusing retry load.
findings.required_resolution: Choose one durable offset authority and document ownership, atomic update semantics and its relationship to PostgreSQL dedup commits. Include that state in the persistence and backup model. Backup must quiesce every writer, including bridge and migrations, and record a non-secret consistency marker linking DB, n8n files, offset state, image lock and encryption-key identifier.
findings.acceptance_test: Crash the bridge before and after n8n acknowledgement and offset commit, restart it, and verify no acknowledged update is lost and duplicates are bounded by the documented window. Restore a backup with real egress disabled and prove offset/dedup consistency before permitting polling.

findings.affected_section: D6, D7 and section 17 — owner bootstrap and workflow import
findings.claim: Owner creation, workflow import, credential binding and activation lack an idempotent lifecycle.
findings.evidence: 07_FULL_PLAN.md:460 requires manual owner/2FA creation and 462 imports workflows without credentials; 650 asks for an exact-version import/export roundtrip. There is no distinction between first boot and an initialized volume, no expected workflow inventory or duplicate policy, and no rule that imported triggers remain inactive until local credentials and real-traffic gates are satisfied.
findings.impact: Repeated setup can create duplicate workflows or leave stale versions. An imported active trigger can execute before credential/allowlist review, while a missing credential or unsupported node may be discovered only during a real test.
findings.required_resolution: Define first-run, owner-pending and initialized states. Import a checksummed exact-version export into isolated mock mode as inactive, validate node types and credential references, reconcile against an expected workflow inventory, and reject duplicates or drift. Bind local credentials separately and activate real triggers only after the manual gate. Make reruns no-op or explicit reconciliation.
findings.acceptance_test: Execute setup twice on a fresh instance and twice on a persistent instance; owner and workflow counts must remain stable. Unsupported nodes, missing credentials and changed workflow hashes must fail before activation. No real trigger may be active before approval, while mock execution and secret-free export/import roundtrip must succeed.

findings.affected_section: D5 and section 17 — image and platform locking
findings.claim: The image lock does not fully define multi-architecture digest semantics or coverage of operational images.
findings.evidence: 07_FULL_PLAN.md:445-450 requires official registries, an exact linux/amd64 digest and pinned build bases; 313 also uses a pinned image for backup. It does not state whether both OCI index and linux/amd64 child-manifest digests are recorded, nor enumerate migration, backup, restore, QA and all Dockerfile stages as mandatory lock entries.
findings.impact: A multi-architecture index, omitted helper image or floating build stage can resolve to different bytes or architecture while the main service inventory still appears pinned. Backup and migration behavior may then drift independently of the application stack.
findings.required_resolution: Create one canonical image lock covering every Compose service, one-shot tool and Dockerfile stage. Record registry/repository, tag as metadata, OCI index digest when present, selected linux/amd64 child digest, config digest, size and provenance. Render every runtime reference as digest plus explicit platform and verify the locally loaded image against the lock before use.
findings.acceptance_test: Parse all rendered Compose files and Dockerfile stages and fail on latest, tag-only, missing platform or an unlocked image. Inspect each loaded image and prove OS/architecture plus manifest/config digests match the lock. An offline restart must use already verified content without tag re-resolution.

findings.affected_section: Sections 5, 10 and D10 — volume isolation and ownership
findings.claim: Project-name separation is asserted without an exact volume naming, collision and ownership contract.
findings.evidence: 07_FULL_PLAN.md:153-157 names volumes; 166-171 requires distinct projects; 319 and 514 require restore under a new project and new volumes. The plan does not say whether Compose-scoped names or explicit global names are used, how pre-existing unlabeled volumes are rejected, or how PostgreSQL/n8n UID, GID and modes are initialized and preserved during archive/restore.
findings.impact: An explicit global volume name can cause local and restore projects to share state despite different project names. Restore or backup tooling running as root can also leave n8n/PostgreSQL data inaccessible to the normal container identity.
findings.required_resolution: Use project-scoped volumes or names parameterized by a validated project identifier, apply ownership labels, and refuse unknown pre-existing volumes. Specify mount destinations, driver assumptions, UID/GID/mode initialization and restore ownership behavior for every volume. Restore cleanup must select only verified project labels.
findings.acceptance_test: Run local, disposable gate and restore projects concurrently; inspect names, labels, mountpoints and container mounts to prove no shared volume. Verify normal non-root service identities can read/write restored state. Deleting the disposable restore project by its approved procedure must leave all local volume IDs and hashes unchanged.

findings.claim: The CLI contract lists status and doctor but does not define stable states or actionable diagnostics.
findings.evidence: 07_FULL_PLAN.md:528-541 lists commands and 543-552 defines generic behavior, but no output schema distinguishes stopped, starting, migration-failed, unhealthy, owner-setup-required, blocked-manual, wrong-mode, key-mismatch or restore-only states.
findings.impact: The owner may retry start or switch modes during a state that requires a manual gate or recovery, increasing downtime and making handover evidence subjective.
findings.required_resolution: Define a versioned machine-readable status schema plus concise human summary. Include intended mode, exact service health, migration state, owner-bootstrap state, image-lock status, persistent-volume identity and permitted next actions without exposing secrets.
findings.acceptance_test: Induce each documented failure and manual-gate state and assert deterministic status/doctor codes, nonzero exits where appropriate, redacted output, and one safe next action. The owner handover must recover from at least a failed migration, unhealthy n8n and stale prior-mode service using only documented commands.

Before analysis I recomputed every manifest file size and SHA-256, the 46234-byte plan SHA-256, and the 1063-byte canonical content aggregate; all matched 00_MANIFEST.json and BUNDLE_ANCHOR.txt.
